_expect.name: Forgotten Wall, Control Tower & Up The Creek Wall

az_forgotten_wall_control_tower_up_the_c.blurb: A cluster of south-facing walls above the Catalina Highway on the lower part of Mount Lemmon: the Forgotten Wall, the Control Tower, and the Up The Creek Wall a short walk beyond it. Sport and trad share the cliff, with most climbs in the 5.10 and 5.11 range. The face climbing is less crimpy than at Windy Point, and several lines go through or around roofs. Cat On A Hot Thin Roof, Tryptophandemonium and Blood Book are among the best known. The southern exposure makes it a good pick on cold, sunny days. Two of the longer routes want a 70 m rope. A creek runs through the approach, and rocks beside it can be icy in cold weather.
az_forgotten_wall_control_tower_up_the_c.parking_note: Pull off beside the highway near milepost 8.6, or use the Thimble Peak Overlook a short way back down the road.
az_forgotten_wall_control_tower_up_the_c.approach: Follow a path up the left flank, then swing right into the drainage above the waterfall. When the creek is running, a higher line is easier. Up The Creek Wall is reached from the foot of the Control Tower by a path that skirts the thick brush. Allow roughly half an hour.

az_casino_cliffs.blurb: Casino Cliffs is the first big wall you reach in Jacks Canyon, on the high plateau south of Winslow. It is a sport crag of steep, pocketed rock, with climbs from easy to hard, though the bulk fall at 5.10 and 5.11 and a handful reach 5.12. Mickey Goes to Vegas, Poker Face and Read 'em and Weep are the standouts. The wall gets morning sun and afternoon shade and is fairly sheltered from wind, so you can often pick a time of day to suit the weather. It is a sociable spot, so expect company at the base.
az_casino_cliffs.parking_note: Drive to the rim campsites above Jacks Canyon and leave the car there; the trail down begins at the campsites.
az_casino_cliffs.approach: From the rim campsites, take the trail down into the canyon, then cross the canyon floor and the wash to reach the base of the wall.

az_dws_west_side.blurb: The west bank of a reservoir stretch of East Clear Creek southeast of Winslow, where sandstone walls rise straight out of deep water. This is deep water soloing: low traverses and boulder problems over the water, plus taller lines that are serious if you are not confident. Most of the boulder problems fall between V1 and V3, with a scattering of trad lines around 5.8 to 5.10 and a few harder ones. Oil Slick, Bear Claw and Last Day Of Summer are good places to start. You get there by boat and must be comfortable swimming. Wind can make paddling tiring, the water is cool, and submerged rocks and shifting sandbars mean testing every landing before you commit.
az_dws_west_side.parking_note: Leave the car at McHood Park, off Highway 99 about five miles from the junction near Winslow.
az_dws_west_side.approach: Launch a boat or kayak at McHood Park and paddle upstream, pass under the bridge, and continue roughly half a mile. The first walls on your right are the west side.

az_upper_sullie_s_north_side.blurb: The north side of Upper Sullivan's, part of a steep basalt gorge east of Highway 89 and north of Chino Valley, near Prescott. The rock is columnar and split by cracks, and nearly everything here is traditional crack climbing, with a few top-rope lines. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.12 and cluster around 5.10, with a fair number of easier cracks, which makes it a good place to practice gear placements. Bring a full rack of cams. Many climbs end at bolted rappel stations. Some of the canyon is a good escape when Prescott is cold and snowy, depending on which side you choose.

az_atlantis_south_side.blurb: The south wall of Atlantis, a deep, narrow cleft in Queen Creek Canyon near Superior. Mostly bolted sport, with a few trad and multipitch lines. It has more vertical and moderate climbing than the north side, with grades from 5.6 up past 5.12 and plenty at 5.9 through 5.11. Ali Cat, First Born, Giggling Marlin and The Trident suit easier grades, while Myrmidon, Slap & Tickle, Unfinished Business, Direct Exposure and Karma Farmer are for stronger climbers. The wall sits in shade in the morning and takes sun in the afternoon. It is one of the few places nearby that works in summer if you start early. Expect the odd loose flake, and company on busy days.
az_atlantis_south_side.parking_note: Heading from Superior toward Globe, pull into the first little lot on the right once you are through the long tunnel. A path leaves from the western end of the lot.
az_atlantis_south_side.approach: A short stroll down to where the canyon opens. Some lines begin just outside that entrance, a couple are above the dam, and most are farther in.

az_north_fin.blurb: A fin of excellent rock at Windy Point on the Catalina Highway, with a high concentration of good routes. Trad and sport mix freely, with most climbs at 5.10 and 5.11 and a few easier ones such as Slippery When Wet, plus several at 5.12 and 5.13. Histoplasmosis, Nang, Air Monsters and When Legends Fly are among the favorites. Most of the climbing is on east-facing walls that fall into shade later in the day, while a few lines at the southern end hold sun into the late afternoon. The walk from the overlook is short.
az_north_fin.parking_note: Park in the Windy Point overlook lot, near mile marker 14 on the Catalina Highway.
az_north_fin.approach: Walk past the restrooms and follow the clear path along the ridge, away from the road, to the big pinnacle called Nancy's Thumb. Descend the steep gully beneath it; the routes line the wall to your right.

az_main_wall_4.blurb: The main concentration of routes in La Milagrosa Canyon, a lower-elevation canyon near Tucson. Smooth orange faces with plenty of crimps and steep sport climbing, mostly 5.10 and 5.11, with a few 5.12s and some trad. The Wizard, Four Play and Community Service are the ones to know. Much of the wall sits in shade, which helps on warm days but can feel cold in winter. It is a winter crag, and the walk in is long by roadside Tucson standards.
az_main_wall_4.parking_note: Leave the car near the big gate at the end of Suzenu Road.
az_main_wall_4.approach: Take the main trail rather than the upper one to the first climbable rock. A minute past an obvious clearing you reach a large rock throne at the base of Community Service, where most routes begin. The first couple of lines start on a platform and are easy to miss.

az_molino_basin_boulders.blurb: A low-elevation bouldering area in a small canyon on the lower Catalina Highway. The rock is water-polished but solid, with good features. Most problems fall between V1 and V4, with a few much harder ones up to double digits. Hammer of Hate (V8) and Block Party (V2+) are the ones people mention. The elevation keeps it comfortable in the cooler months. Some landings can sit under standing water, so check before you pad up.
az_molino_basin_boulders.parking_note: Leave the car at the Molino Canyon Vista lot beside the Catalina Highway, roughly a mile short of the Molino Basin Campground turnoff.
az_molino_basin_boulders.approach: Head south from the lot on the wide path for a couple of minutes, then take a smaller trail down to the wash and cross it. Scramble down a short step, pick up the trail to It Cliff, and follow it to the far end; a trail there drops you just downstream of Boxcar Boulder and Hammer of Hate.

az_chimney_rock.blurb: A large standalone tower beside the Catalina Highway, on its western side close to mile marker 11, in the Bear Canyon sector of Mount Lemmon. Nearly all of the climbing is traditional and sits on the broad east face, with a couple of very hard sport lines on the back. Grades run from 5.7 to 5.12, mostly 5.9 to 5.11. Centerpiece, Crows Nest and Single Lens Reflex are among the best. A long, moderate multipitch line up the formation is a popular way to learn that craft. Mind the traffic and falling rock around the base.
az_chimney_rock.parking_note: Use the large pullout on the right just beyond mile marker 11, driving uphill.
az_chimney_rock.approach: Either walk down the highway about a quarter mile to the foot of the east face and scramble a short fourth-class step onto the rock, or cross to the large culvert, climb the slope beside it to an upper ledge, and bushwhack south about a quarter mile.

az_sundog_wall.blurb: A wall in The Notch, among the Peavine Trail crags in the Granite Dells north of Prescott, where weathered Precambrian granite forms rounded, folded outcrops. The climbing here is almost all traditional, mostly cracks, with a couple of top-rope lines. Grades start around 5.6 and reach 5.13, with the largest group at 5.10 and a good number at 5.9. Some cracks are wide and call for big cams. The crags are reached on foot from the Peavine Trail, a rail trail beside Watson Lake, and a bicycle can speed up the trip in.
